newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ fraud studies clear ATN TV and all directors.
newsitem.headline: NZ fraud studies clear ATN TV and all directors.

text.p: New Zealand's Serious Fraud Office and the Registrar of Companies on Thursday both exonerated the directors of Maori broadcaster Aotearoa Television Network (ATN) and said they planned no further action on the company.
New Zealand First MP Tukuroirangi Morgan was a director of ATN prior to joining parliament after last year's general election.

"It is my carefully considered view after weighing all material available to me that the evidence here falls short of establishing any serious or complex fraud on the part of any of the persons associated with Aotearoa or its associated company Pumanawa to justify criminal charges," the acting director of the Serious Fraud Office said in a statement.
Acting SFO director Judge Ron Jamieson commented in an eight-page report that "within Aotearoa there were what can only be described as lax arrangements for the expenditure of company funds".
For many months New Zealand's media have been reporting allegations about the way Morgan appeared to spend company money on personal clothing while at ATN.
The SFO said that "in the absence of much clearer controls it would be vitrually impossible to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that any particular expenditure was not authorised".
Therefore, as it could not identify whether or not spending had been properly authorised, its observations were limited to the level of spending.
It noted that Morgan and fellow executive producer Morehu McDonald's spending on personal clothing "was clearly disproportionate to that of the other executive producers".

"However, because there was no obligation to account for expenditure either to Aotearoa or to TMP (Te Mangai Paho, the funder of Maori broadcasting), except in the most general terms, I cannot say it was criminal," Jamieson went on

He added that the evidence on travel spending by Morgan "could not support a criminal charge" and, in the absence of any definition of the role of executive producer, he could not say that Morgan's assertion to have remained in this capacity until the final months of 1996 was untrue.
The Registrar of Companies, Neville Harris, said in a separate statement his office was not contemplating any further action following its investigation into ATN Ltd.
Although it questioned some of the book-keeping practices at the company it did not believe these involved breaches of the companies act.
Both agencies said they did not wish to make any further comment on the matter.
New Zealand First leader and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters has said Morgan's future in the NZ First caucus would be left open until the SFO reported.
Peters, travelling in Australia, was not initially available for comment and Prime Minister Jim Bolger told reporters in parliament he did not intend to comment on the matter yet.

Morgan was a director and presenter at ATN before being elected to parliament in October 1996. He has said he had authority to spend the money, including $89 on a pair of boxer shorts, but staff at the station had denied this.

Opposition MPs stepped up their calls for his resignation last month after Morgan admitted seeking payment for a television interview about the ATN affair and then misleading Peters about his knowledge of it.
Meanwhile, Morgan has sued Labour MP Trevor Mallard for comments he made at a press conference about the ATN affair.
